summary: Proposes a method for managing how the bits of an IPv6 address block are divided up for subnets or customers. It lets an organization postpone the final choice on how many bits go to each level, which makes later growth easier. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3531 offers a way to divide an address block into parts that can still be resized later. Each part is filled in from the side that is not next to a boundary, so the bits nearest a boundary are used last and the boundary itself can still be moved. An organisation can therefore postpone deciding exactly how many bits each of its subnets or customers should get.

questions: how to plan ipv6 address space
how to allocate ipv6 addresses flexibly
what is the centermost bit assignment method
how does rfc 3531 improve on rfc 1219
subtitle: How to split an address block into parts while keeping the boundaries movable later

tldr.problem: An address block is usually cut into pieces for each customer or subnet, and the sizes guessed at the start often turn out wrong. Once the bits are assigned, the authority cannot allocate contiguous addresses because they have already gone to somebody else.
tldr.mechanism: The scheme assigns the leftmost part of the block from the left, the rightmost part from the right, and the parts in between from the middle outwards. The bits closest to each boundary are used last, so a boundary can still move while there are free bits beside it.
tldr.outcome: A provider can hand out more customers later, and a customer can change its mind about the size of its own customers, until the reserved bits are used up. The scheme generalises the IPv4 method of RFC 1219 and works for IPv4 and IPv6 alike.

facts.label: Parts of an address
facts.value: p1 to pN, each of a possibly different length

facts.label: Assignment orders
facts.value: Leftmost for p1, rightmost for pN, centermost for the parts in between

facts.label: Example customer bits
facts.value: 8 bits for the provider's customers, 10 more bits for one of them

today: RFC 3531 is an Informational memo published in April 2003, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It offers a way of planning an address block that keeps the option of changing the boundaries later, and it gives registries no new rules about how to assign ranges to their customers.

sections.title: Why the Bit Boundaries Matter
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses have a flexible structure for address assignments. This lets registries, internet service providers, network designers and others assign address ranges to organisations and networks on different criteria, such as the size of networks and the estimated growth rate. Often the initial assignment does not scale well, because a small network becomes larger than expected and needs more addresses, while the assignment authority cannot allocate contiguous addresses because they were already assigned to another network.

RFC 1219 describes an allocation scheme for IPv4 where address space is kept unallocated between the leftmost bits of the subnet part and the rightmost bits of the host part of the address. This enables the network designer to change the subnet mask without renumbering, for the central bits that are not allocated.

This document generalises that scheme by extending the algorithm so it can be applied to any part of an IP address, assigned by any level of authority such as registries, internet service providers of any level, or organisations. It can be used for both IPv4 and IPv6. The document does not provide any recommendation to registries on how to assign address ranges to their customers.
sections.plainLanguage: An address block is usually cut into pieces, one per customer or subnet. The trouble is that the sizes guessed at the start often turn out wrong, and a cut that is already made is hard to move. This scheme keeps the bits near each cut free for as long as possible, so the cuts can still be moved later.

sections.title: The Scheme
sections.content:
The scheme defines the parts of an IP address as p1, p2, p3, ... pN in order, so that an IP address is composed of these parts contiguously. The boundary between each part is based on the prefix assigned by the next level of authority. Part p1 is the leftmost part and is probably assigned to a registry. Part p2 can be allocated to a large internet service provider or to a national registry. Part p3 can be allocated to a large customer or a smaller provider. Each part can be of a different length, and l(pX) is the length of part X.

The algorithm for allocating addresses is as follows. For the leftmost part p1, addresses are assigned using the leftmost bits first. For the rightmost part pN, addresses are assigned using the rightmost bits first. For all the other parts, the centre parts, an arbitrary boundary is predefined as a prefix and addresses are assigned using the centre bits first of the part being assigned.

This algorithm grows the assigned bits in such a way that it keeps the unassigned bits near the boundary of the parts. The prefix between any two parts can therefore be changed forward or backward later on, up to the assigned bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is split into contiguous parts, one for each level of authority. The leftmost part is handed out from the left, the rightmost part from the right, and the parts in between from the middle outwards. The bits closest to each boundary are the ones used last, so a boundary can still be moved while there are free bits next to it.

sections.title: Leftmost, Rightmost and Centermost
sections.content:
Leftmost assignment mirrors binary counting. The order runs 00000000, 10000000, 01000000, 11000000, 00100000, 10100000, 01100000, 11100000, 00010000, and so on, so the first bit to vary is the leftmost one.

Rightmost assignment is plain binary counting from the right. The order runs 00000000, 00000001, 00000010, 00000011, 00000100, 00000101, 00000110, 00000111, 00001000, and so on.

Centermost assignment, used for a part between the first and the last, starts in the middle. The first round is to select only the middle bit, picking the bit following the centre when there is an even number of bits. All combinations using the selected bits that have not yet been created are then created. A new round begins by adding one more bit to the set, adding the preceding bit in even rounds and the subsequent bit in odd rounds, and the process repeats until there are no more bits to consider. For an eight-bit part the order runs 00000000, 00001000, 00010000, 00011000, 00000100, 00001100, 00010100, 00011100, 00100000, and so on.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three orders. The first part is filled from the left, the last part from the right, and the parts in between start in the middle and spread outwards one bit at a time, alternating between the bit above and the bit below the middle.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The example starts with a provider that has been assigned the 3ffe:0b00/24 prefix and wants to assign prefixes to its connected networks. It anticipates in the foreseeable future a maximum of 256 customers consuming 8 bits. One of those customers, named C2, anticipates a maximum of 1024 customer assignments under it, consuming 10 other bits.

P1 assigns address space to its customers using leftmost bits, so C1 is assigned 10000000, C2 is assigned 01000000 and C3 is assigned 11000000. C2 then assigns address space to its own customers, C2C1, C2C2 and so on, using centermost bits, so C2C1 is assigned 0000010000, C2C2 is assigned 0000100000 and C2C3 is assigned 0000110000. Customers of C2 can use centermost bits for maximum flexibility, and the last aggregators, which should be a network in a site, are assigned using rightmost bits.

Putting all the bits together for C2C3 gives 00111111 11111110 00001011 01000000 00001100 00, where the two rightmost groups are the growing bits. By using this method P1 is able to expand the number of customers, and the customers are able to modify their first assumptions about the size of their own customers, until the reserved bits are assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example shows a provider handing out 8 bits to its customers from the left, one of those customers handing out 10 bits to its own customers from the middle, and the site at the end using bits from the right. Each level can grow until the bits reserved for growth run out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document has one sentence on the subject: address assignment does not seem to have any specific security consideration.

That is the whole of the section. Nothing else in the RFC treats security, and the document says nothing about the trust relationships between the parties that assign and use the addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says that address assignment raises no security question of its own, and nothing further.
